Think of "untoward" as a word that describes something that is unexpected AND unwelcome — something that shouldn't be happening, or something that is out of place in a way that causes discomfort, trouble, or embarrassment.

It sits at the intersection of two feelings: "That's not right" and "That's not good."

"Untoward" is used in two closely related ways, and understanding both will give you a complete grip on the word.

Sense 1 — Something improper or inappropriate

Here, "untoward" describes behavior, remarks, or actions that are not suitable for the situation — things that cross a line of decency, politeness, or social acceptability.

"She made sure none of the guests behaved in an untoward manner during the formal dinner."

"He denied making any untoward advances toward his colleague."

In this sense, "untoward" is close in meaning to improper, unseemly, or inappropriate — but it carries an extra shade of meaning: the behavior is not just wrong, it is also jarring and out of place, like something that disturbs the normal order of things.

Sense 2 — An event or circumstance that is unfavorable or problematic

Here, "untoward" describes an unexpected event or situation that causes inconvenience, difficulty, or harm. It is something that was not supposed to happen and makes things harder or worse.

"The surgery went smoothly, and there were no untoward complications."

"Despite the untoward circumstances, the team managed to complete the project on time."

In this sense, "untoward" is close to adverse, unfortunate, or inconvenient — but again, with that extra layer of meaning: it wasn't planned, it wasn't welcome, and it disrupts the way things should go.

Notice that in both senses, something deviates from what is expected or acceptable and creates a problem as a result. That is the heart of "untoward":

Something untoward = something unexpected that is also wrong, inappropriate, or harmful in some way.

It is never a neutral word. "Untoward" always signals that something is off — and that this "offness" matters.

By far the most frequently used construction with this word is "nothing untoward." You will encounter this phrase constantly in everyday writing, news, and conversation. It means: nothing unexpected, suspicious, improper, or problematic happened.

"The police searched the apartment but found nothing untoward."

"She reviewed the documents carefully and noticed nothing untoward."

"He assured them that nothing untoward had occurred during his absence."

This phrase is often used to put someone's worries to rest — it says: you can relax, everything was normal, there was no cause for concern.
The Feeling and Tone of the Word

"Untoward" is a formal and somewhat literary word. You will not often hear it in casual conversation, but you will regularly see it in:

  • News reports ("no untoward incidents were reported")
  • Medical and legal writing ("untoward side effects," "untoward conduct")
  • Formal statements and official communication
  • Literature and careful, polished writing

When a writer chooses "untoward" over a simpler word like "bad" or "wrong," they are being deliberate and precise. The word feels measured and controlled — it doesn't shout; it quietly signals that something is not as it should be.
How It Differs from Similar Words

• "Inappropriate" focuses purely on something not fitting the situation. "Untoward" includes the added idea of something being unexpected or disrupting normal order.
  • "Adverse" focuses on something being harmful or unfavorable. "Untoward" can mean this too, but it also covers the improper/unseemly meaning that "adverse" does not.
  • "Unfortunate" is softer and more sympathetic. "Untoward" is more clinical and precise — it doesn't ask you to feel sorry; it just signals that something is out of order.

What it meansUnexpected and unwelcome — either improper/inappropriate (of behavior) or adverse/problematic (of events/circumstances)
The common threadSomething that deviates from what is acceptable or expected, in a way that causes trouble or discomfort
Most common use"Nothing untoward" — meaning nothing suspicious, inappropriate, or problematic happened

If you remember only one thing: "untoward" = unexpected + unwelcome, and it quietly signals that something is not right with how things are unfolding. That single idea will serve you correctly every time you encounter or use this word.
